summary: This informational memo defines MIB objects for managing RADIUS accounting clients. It replaces RFC 2620 by deprecating the table limited to IPv4 addresses and adding one that supports version-neutral IP addresses, keeping the remaining objects.

eli5.summary: Accounting clients send in the record of who used the network and for how long. This is a dashboard for watching those senders, updated to handle newer style addresses.

subtitle: A management database for watching how a RADIUS accounting client talks to its servers, now able to hold IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: The earlier RADIUS accounting client MIB, RFC 2620, could only record server addresses in an IPv4-only format.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4670 deprecates the IPv4-only table and adds a new table, radiusAccServerExtTable, that uses version-neutral address types, while carrying the other objects forward and adding UNITS and REFERENCE clauses.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2620. It is an Informational memo, and its server-side partner is RFC 4671.

today: RFC 4670 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 2620, and it has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata. The matching server-side MIB is RFC 4671.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 4670 defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) used with network management protocols. Its objects relate to the RADIUS accounting client defined in RFC 2866. A MIB is a virtual information store that is generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), and this module is written in SMIv2.

In RADIUS accounting, clients send Accounting-Requests and servers reply with Accounting-Responses. Network Access Server (NAS) devices typically implement the client function, so they would be expected to implement this client MIB.
sections.eli5: This is a set of gauges that a network manager can read to see how an accounting sender is doing.

sections.title: What Changed From RFC 2620
sections.content:
This memo obsoletes RFC 2620. It deprecates the radiusAccServerTable table and adds a new table, radiusAccServerExtTable, which contains radiusAccServerInetAddressType, radiusAccServerInetAddress and radiusAccClientServerInetPortNumber. The point of the new objects is to support version-neutral IP addressing formats.

The RFC follows a recommendation quoted from RFC 4001: when revising a MIB module with IPv4-specific tables, define new tables with the version-neutral textual conventions, make the new tables current and mark the old ones deprecated. Keeping multiple similar tables for different IP versions is strongly discouraged. The remaining objects from RFC 2620 are carried forward, and UNITS and REFERENCE clauses are added to selected objects.
sections.eli5: The old address box only fit short addresses. The authors added a bigger box that fits any kind, and put a 'do not use' sticker on the old one.

sections.title: Structure of the Module
sections.content:
The module contains two scalars plus a table listing the RADIUS accounting servers with which the client shares a secret. Each row stands for one server. The scalars are radiusAccClientInvalidServerAddresses, which counts Accounting-Response packets received from unknown addresses, and radiusAccClientIdentifier, the NAS-Identifier of the client (which is not necessarily the same as sysName).

An entity can play both roles. A RADIUS proxy may be a server to some clients and a client to some servers, and such an entity is expected to support both the client MIB defined here and the server MIB in RFC 4671. The module sits under the RADIUS MIB branch mib-2 67.
sections.eli5: Some machines both send records and receive them, like a mail room that is also a customer. They keep both dashboards.

sections.title: The Per-Server Counters
sections.content:
Each server row tracks request and response activity. Examples are requests sent (not counting retransmissions), retransmissions, responses, malformed responses, bad authenticators, pending requests, timeouts, unknown types, packets dropped, and the round trip time of the most recent matching request and response.

The RFC states the relationship between them in a comment: Requests = Responses + PendingRequests + ClientTimeouts. Malformed responses include packets with an invalid length, but bad authenticators and unknown types are not counted as malformed. The new table adds radiusAccClientCounterDiscontinuity, the time in centiseconds since the last discontinuity in the counters, such as a reinitialization of the accounting client module.
sections.eli5: Each server gets a scorecard: how many letters were sent, how many answers came back, how many were garbled or never arrived.

sections.title: Keeping the Deprecated Table
sections.content:
A managed entity MAY keep supporting the deprecated table in two cases: it supports only IPv4 addresses, or it supports both IPv4 and IPv6 and keeps the old table for older management stations. The second case SHOULD only be used when the addresses in the new table are in IPv4 format and can be represented accurately in both tables.

Entities SHOULD NOT create rows in the deprecated table for a server that does not have an IPv4 address, and SHOULD NOT return wrong addresses or SNMP access errors for IPv4-only objects. If the same server appears in both tables, the row indexes SHOULD be the same so management applications can match them.
sections.eli5: You may keep the old dashboard for old viewers, but it must never show a wrong address. If the old and new boards list the same server, they should use the same row number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in this MIB has a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create, so a correct implementation cannot be altered through SNMP SET operations. Some objects are still sensitive: the server address objects could help someone attack the accounting server, and the port number objects could help someone impersonate the client.

Every object in this MIB is read-only except where noted, and the RFC points to SNMPv3 for protection. It recommends that implementers consider the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.

The RFC says it is important to control even GET access to these objects.
sections.eli5: You cannot change the dashboard, but it shows where the servers live, so only the right people should be allowed to look at it.
